questions.question: In the complex conjugate root theorem, what condition on the polynomial is essential?
options: The polynomial must have integer coefficients.
The polynomial must have degree two.
The polynomial must have no real roots.
The polynomial must have real coefficients.

questions.question: What is meant by the interpretation that complex roots of real polynomials come in pairs?
options: Every root is repeated twice.
Every real root has a distinct real partner.
Every non-real complex root is accompanied by its complex conjugate.
Every polynomial with real coefficients has exactly two roots.

questions.question: Why does the complex conjugate root theorem help explain why an odd-degree real polynomial must have at least one real root?
options: Non-real roots occur in pairs, leaving a real root in odd degree.
Because a non-real root forces its negative to be a root.
Because every odd-degree polynomial has exactly one real root.
Because each conjugate pair counts as one root.

questions.question: How does the complex conjugate root theorem treat a real root written as a + ib?
options: It is outside the theorem because a and b must be non-zero.
It gives the same root again when b = 0.
It forces a second distinct real root.
It shows that the polynomial has no non-real roots.

questions.question: A real square matrix has odd size. What can be concluded about its eigenvalues?
options: All its eigenvalues are real.
It has at least one real eigenvalue.
Its non-real eigenvalues cannot occur in conjugate pairs.
Its determinant must be zero.

questions.question: If $a+\mathrm{i}b$ is a non-real root of a real polynomial, what companion root is guaranteed?
options: $-a+\mathrm{i}b$
$-a-\mathrm{i}b$
$b+\mathrm{i}a$
$a-\mathrm{i}b$

questions.question: A real polynomial has $5-2\mathrm{i}$ as a root. Which root is also guaranteed?
options: $-5-2\mathrm{i}$
$5+2\mathrm{i}$
$-5+2\mathrm{i}$
$2-5\mathrm{i}$

questions.question: A real polynomial of degree $3$ has the roots $2+\mathrm{i}$ and $2-\mathrm{i}$. What can be concluded about its third root, counted with multiplicity?
options: It must be real.
It must be $2$.
It must be non-real.
It can be real or non-real.

questions.question: A polynomial $P$ with real coefficients has the root $\lambda=3+2\mathrm{i}$. By the complex conjugate root theorem, $(z-\lambda)(z-\overline{\lambda})$ is a quadratic factor of $P$ with real coefficients. Which quadratic is it?
Let $P$ be a polynomial of degree $4$ with real coefficients, so that it has $4$ complex roots counted with multiplicity. Which number of real roots, counted with multiplicity, is impossible for $P$?
